edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 2, Paris 1844), De resurrectione carnis, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.locus: On the Resurrection of the Flesh VII
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Sed dilutior videatur auctoritas carnis, quia non ipsam proprie manus divina tractavit, sicut limum. Quando in hoc tractavit limum, ut postmodum caro fieret ex limo, carnis utique negotium gessit. Sed adhuc velim discas, quando et quomodo caro floruerit ex limo. Neque enim, ut quidam volunt, illae pelliciae tunicae, quas Adam et Eva, paradisum exuti, induerunt, ipsae erunt carnis ex limo reformatio; cum aliquanto prius et Adam, substantiae suae traducem in foemina jam carnem recognoverit: Hoc nunc os ex ossibus meis, et caro ex carne mea; et ipsa delibatio masculi in foeminam carne suppleta sit, limo, opinor, supplenda, si Adam adhuc limus. Obliteratus igitur et devoratus est limus in carnem. Quando? cum factus est homo in animam vivam, de Dei flatu, vapore scilicet idoneo torrere quodammodo limum in aliam qualitatem; quasi in testam, ita in carnem. Sic et figulo licet argillam temperato ignis adflatu in materiam robustiorem recorporare, et in aliam ex alia fingere speciem, aptiorem pristina, et sui jam generis ac nominis. Nam etsi scriptum est: Numquid argilla dicet figulo? id est, homo Deo; et si Apostolus, In testaceis, ait, vasculis; tamen et argilla homo, quia limus ante; et testa caro, quia ex limo per adflatus divini vaporem, quam postea pelliciae tunicae, id est, cutes superductae, vestierunt. Usque adeo, si detraxeris cutem, nudaveris carnem. Ita, quod hodie spolium efficitur, si detrahatur, hoc fuit indumentum cum superstruebatur. Hinc et Apostolus, circumcisionem despoliationem carnis appellans, tunicam cutem confirmavit. Haec cum ita sint, habes et limum de manu Dei gloriosum, et carnem de afflatu Dei gloriosiorem, quo pariter caro et limi rudimenta deposuit, et animae ornamenta suscepit. Non es diligentior Deo, uti tu quidem scythicas et indicas gemmas, et rubentis maris grana candentia; non plumbo, non aere, non ferro, ne argento quoque oblaquees; sed electissimo et insuper operosissimo descrobes auro; vinis item et unguentis pretiosissimis quibusque vasculorum prius congruentiam cures; proinde perfectae ferruginis gladiis vaginarum adaeques dignitatem: Deus vero animae suae umbram, spiritus sui auram, oris sui operam, vilissimo alicui commiserit capulo, et indigne collocando utique damnaverit. Collocavit autem, an potius inseruit et immiscuit carni, tanta quidem concretione, ut incertum haberi possit utrumne caro animam, an carnem anima circumferat; utrumne animae caro, an anima appareat carni. Sed et magis animam invehi atque dominari credendum est, ut magis Deo proximam. Hoc quoque ad gloriam carnis exuberat, quod proximam Deo et continet, et ipsius dominationis compotem praestat. Quem enim naturae usum, quem mundi fructum, quem elementorum saporem, non per carnem anima depascitur? quidni? per quam omni instrumento sensum fulta est, visu, auditu, gustu, odoratu, contactu; per quam divina potestate respersa est, nihil non sermone perficiens vel tacite praemisso. Et sermo enim de organo carnis est; artes per carnem; studia, ingenia, per carnem; opera, negotia, officia, per carnem: atque adeo totum vivere animae carnis est, ut non vivere animae nihil aliud sit, quam a carne devertere: sic etiam ipsum mori carnis est, cujus et vivere. Porro, si universa per carnem subjacent animae, carni quoque subjaceant, per quod utaris, necesse est. Ita caro, dum ministra et famula animae deputatur, consors et cohaeredes invenitur. Si temporalium, cur non et aeternorum?
pass_a_gloss: But the authority of the flesh seems more diluted because the divine hand did not directly handle it, as it did the clay. When, however, it handled the clay, so that later flesh would be made from the clay, it was certainly dealing with the flesh's business. But I still want you to learn when and how the flesh flourished from the clay. For it is not, as some people want, the case that those skin tunics, which Adam and Eve, after they were expelled from paradise, put on, will be the reformation of the flesh from the clay; since Adam had already, before this, recognized the flesh in the woman, who was made from his substance: This bone is now from my bones, and this flesh is from my flesh. And this consideration of the male in the female flesh was supplemented, I think, by the clay, if Adam was still clay. Therefore, the clay was obliterated and devoured by the flesh. When? When man was made into a living soul, from God's breath, that is, from a certain vapor that was suitable for drying the clay in a certain way into another quality, as if into earthenware, so into flesh. Just as a potter is also able to re-form clay, tempered by fire, into a stronger material, and to shape one form into another, more suitable than the first, and of its own kind and name. For although it is written: Will the clay say to the potter? that is, will man say to God? and if the Apostle says: In earthen vessels; nevertheless, the clay is also man, because it was clay before; and the earthenware is flesh, because it is from the clay through the divine vapor, which was breathed upon it, and afterwards the skin tunics, that is, the skins, were put on. To such an extent that if you remove the skin, you will strip the flesh bare. So, what is now a spoil, if it is removed, was a garment when it was put on. From this, the Apostle also, calling circumcision a stripping of the flesh, confirmed that the skin is a tunic. Since these things are so, you have both the clay, glorious from God's hand, and the flesh, more glorious from God's breath, by which equally the flesh and the clay's rudiments were laid aside, and the soul's ornaments were taken up. You are not more diligent than God, so that you, indeed, adorn scythian and indian gems, and the shining grains of the red sea, not with lead, not with copper, not with iron, not even with silver, but with the most select and most laborious gold; and you also take care to anoint the vessels with the most precious wines and ointments; accordingly, you adapt the dignity of the perfectly forged swords to the sheaths: but God, indeed, committed the shadow of his soul, the breeze of his spirit, the work of his mouth, to a most vile vessel, and, placing it unworthily, condemned it, as it were. But he placed, or rather inserted and mixed, the soul into the flesh, with such a great concretion, that it can be uncertain whether the flesh carries the soul, or the soul carries the flesh; whether the soul appears to the flesh, or the flesh to the soul. But it is also more believable that the soul is carried and dominates, since it is closer to God. This also overflows with glory for the flesh, that it is closest to God and contains it, and provides a share in its dominion. For what use of nature, what fruit of the world, what taste of the elements, does the soul not enjoy through the flesh? Why not? Through which the soul is supported by every instrument of sense, by sight, by hearing, by taste, by smell, by touch; through which the soul is sprinkled with divine power, accomplishing nothing without speech, or with silent permission. And speech, indeed, is from the organ of the flesh; arts through the flesh; studies, talents, through the flesh; works, businesses, duties, through the flesh: and so the whole life of the soul is the flesh, so that not to live is nothing other than to turn away from the flesh: so also the death of the flesh is its own, whose life is also its own. Furthermore, if all things are subject to the soul through the flesh, it is necessary that they also be subject to the flesh, through which you use them. So the flesh, while it is appointed as a minister and servant of the soul, is found to be a partner and co-heir. If it is so with temporal things, why not also with eternal things?

refers to the act of cutting away the foreskin
despoliationem refers to the act of stripping away
scythicas refers to gems from Scythia, and indicas refers to gems from India

pass_b_english: The flesh's authority seems weaker because the divine hand didn't handle it directly, as it did the clay. Yet when God worked the clay so that flesh would later come from it, he was already conducting the flesh's business. I still want you to learn when and how the flesh flowered from that clay. Some claim the skin tunics Adam and Eve put on after being expelled from Paradise represent the flesh's reformation from clay, but that's false. Adam had already recognized flesh in the woman formed from his substance long before that, declaring, "This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh" (Gen 2:23). That recognition of the male in the female, filled out with flesh, had to be supplemented by clay, I think, if Adam was still clay at that point. So the clay was obliterated and consumed into flesh. When? When man became a living soul by God's breath—a vapor suited to bake the clay into a different quality, as a potter fires clay into earthenware. Just as a potter reforms fire-tempered clay into stronger material, shaping one form into another more fitting than the first, now of its own kind and name. Scripture asks, "Will the clay say to the potter?"—meaning, will man challenge God? (Isa 64:8). And the Apostle calls us "earthen vessels" (2 Cor 4:7). Yet clay is also man, because it was clay first; and earthenware is flesh, because it comes from clay through the divine vapor breathed into it, which the skin tunics—meaning skins—later covered. To the point that if you strip off the skin, you lay the flesh bare. What becomes spoil when removed was a garment when put on. That's why the Apostle, calling circumcision a stripping of the flesh, confirmed the skin is a tunic. Given all this, you have clay made glorious by God's hand, and flesh made more glorious by God's breath—by which both laid aside the rudiments of clay and took on the soul's ornaments. You aren't more careful than God. You set Scythian and Indian gems, the glowing pearls of the Red Sea, not in lead, copper, iron, or even silver, but in the most select and painstakingly worked gold. You anoint vessels with the costliest wines and ointments. You match the dignity of perfectly forged swords to their sheaths. Yet God entrusted the shadow of his soul, the breeze of his spirit, the work of his mouth, to the vilest vessel—and by placing it so unworthily, condemned it, as it were. But he placed, or rather inserted and blended, the soul into flesh with such intimate concretion that it's uncertain whether flesh carries soul or soul carries flesh; whether soul appears to flesh or flesh to soul. Still, we must believe the soul is borne along and dominates, since it stands nearer to God. This too redounds to the flesh's glory: it lies closest to God, contains him, and shares in his dominion. For what use of nature, what fruit of the world, what taste of the elements does the soul not enjoy through the flesh? Through which the soul is served by every instrument of sense—sight, hearing, taste, smell, touch; through which the soul is sprinkled with divine power, accomplishing nothing without speech, even if silently permitted. Speech itself comes from the flesh's organ; arts through the flesh; studies, talents, through the flesh; works, business, duties, through the flesh. The soul's entire life is the flesh, so that not to live is nothing other than turning away from the flesh. Dying, too, belongs to the flesh, whose life it also is. If all things are subject to the soul through the flesh, they must also be subject to the flesh, through which you use them. So the flesh, though appointed minister and servant of the soul, is found to be partner and co-heir. If this holds for temporal things, why not for eternal ones?

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text, including the complex theological arguments regarding the relationship between clay, flesh, and the soul. All scripture citations (Gen 2:23, Isa 64:8, 2 Cor 4:7) are correctly identified and applied to the relevant clauses. The distinction between 'dilutior' (more diluted/weaker) and the potter's metaphor is well-preserved.

The Latin text is correctly translated, with accurate citations and faithful representation of the original meaning.
